people.name: Appius Claudius Caudex
people.summary: Consul in 264 who led the first Roman army across the Straits of Messina, beginning the First Punic War; probably a son of Appius Claudius Caecus.

people.name: Manius Valerius Messalla
people.summary: Consul in 263 who forced Hiero II into alliance, took the cognomen Messalla from Messana, displayed the first battle painting in the Curia and brought a Catanian sundial to Rome; censor 252.

people.name: Gaius Duilius
people.summary: Novus homo, consul in 260, victor of Mylae, Rome's first naval triumph; honoured with the Columna Rostrata and a torch and flute player to escort him home at night. Censor 258.

people.name: Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Asina
people.summary: Son of Scipio Barbatus; consul 260, captured with his squadron at Lipara and nicknamed Asina; ransomed, he took Panormus as consul again in 254 and triumphed.

people.name: Lucius Cornelius Scipio
people.summary: Son of Scipio Barbatus and brother of Asina; consul 259, captured Aleria in Corsica and dedicated a temple to the Tempestates; censor 258. His verse epitaph survives in the Tomb of the Scipios.

people.name: Aulus Atilius Calatinus
people.summary: Consul 258 and 254, captor of Panormus, and in 249 the first dictator to lead an army outside Italy. His epitaph called him by common consent the foremost man of Rome.

people.name: Marcus Atilius Regulus
people.summary: Consul 256, victor at Ecnomus and Adys, whose harsh terms to Carthage were rejected; defeated and captured by Xanthippus at Tunes in 255. Roman legend made him a martyr of fides who returned to Carthage to die under torture.
people.detail: Polybius (1.35) treats him as an example of the instability of fortune and knows nothing of the embassy and torture, which appear in later Roman writers (Cicero, Horace, Livy's epitome). Diodorus' story of his widow's revenge on Carthaginian prisoners suggests the torture legend arose to justify her actions.
people.death: died in Carthaginian captivity, c. 250; torture story probably legend
people.debate: Embassy and torture legend versus Polybius' silence.

people.name: Lucius Caecilius Metellus
people.summary: Victor at Panormus (250) who captured and paraded the Carthaginian elephants; consul 251 and 247, pontifex maximus from 243, dictator 224. Blinded rescuing the Palladium from the burning temple of Vesta in 241.
people.detail: His son's funeral eulogy, quoted by Pliny (7.139-140), lists the ten greatest things a Roman could achieve and claims he achieved them all: first warrior, best orator, bravest general, greatest commands, highest honour, supreme wisdom, foremost senator, great wealth honestly gained, many children, and fame. It is a key text of Roman aristocratic values.

people.name: Publius Claudius Pulcher
people.summary: Consul 249, who threw the sacred chickens overboard before losing the fleet at Drepana; mocked the Senate by naming his freedman dictator, and was condemned and fined. Died before 246.

people.name: Gaius Lutatius Catulus
people.summary: Consul 242, who trained the new privately funded fleet and destroyed the Carthaginian relief fleet at the Aegates Islands on 10 March 241, ending the First Punic War; negotiated the treaty that bears his name.

people.name: Gaius Flaminius
people.summary: The most controversial politician of the inter-war years: as tribune (232) he distributed the ager Gallicus, as praetor (227) he was first governor of Sicily, as consul (223) he defeated the Insubres and triumphed against the Senate's will, and as censor (220) he built the Via Flaminia and Circus Flaminius. He supported the Lex Claudia. Killed at Lake Trasimene in his second consulship.
people.detail: The hostile tradition, rooted in Fabius Pictor and amplified by Livy, portrays him as an impious demagogue who despised the auspices. Modern scholars see a successful novus homo with a strong popular base, and the senatorial verdict as partly retrospective scapegoating for Trasimene.
people.death: killed by an Insubrian horseman at Lake Trasimene
scholarship: Feig Vishnia, State, Society and Popular Leaders in Mid-Republican Rome (1996)

people.name: Marcus Claudius Marcellus
people.summary: Five times consul, winner of the last spolia opima at Clastidium (222), defender of Nola, conqueror of Syracuse (212) and the most aggressive Roman commander against Hannibal; Posidonius called him the sword of Rome to Fabius' shield. Killed in an ambush near Venusia in his fifth consulship.
people.detail: His removal of Syracusan art to Rome was remembered as the start of Roman passion for Greek art. He dedicated a double temple of Honos and Virtus. Plutarch's Life, paired with Pelopidas, preserves much of the family tradition.
people.death: killed in a Numidian ambush near Venusia

people.name: Quintus Fabius Maximus
people.summary: Five times consul and twice dictator, the architect of the strategy of attrition against Hannibal after Trasimene, which earned him the name Cunctator ('Delayer'). He recovered Tarentum in 209, became princeps senatus, and opposed Scipio's invasion of Africa.
people.detail: Nicknamed Verrucosus for a wart on his lip and Ovicula ('little lamb') as a mild child. He was augur for 62 years. Ennius' line 'one man by delaying restored the state to us' fixed his reputation. His opposition to Scipio, whom he saw as reckless and Hellenising, is sometimes read as factional rivalry.

people.name: Lucius Aemilius Paullus
people.summary: Consul 219, victor in the Second Illyrian War over Demetrius of Pharos, and consul 216, killed at Cannae. Roman tradition, shaped by his descendants and Polybius' patrons, made him the cautious consul overruled by his rash plebeian colleague Varro.
people.debate: Polybius' favourable portrait reflects his friendship with Paullus' grandson Scipio Aemilianus.

people.name: Gaius Terentius Varro
people.summary: Novus homo, consul 216, who commanded on the day of Cannae and escaped. The Senate thanked him for not despairing of the Republic, and he held commands and embassies for years afterwards, which casts doubt on the hostile tradition that he alone caused the disaster.
people.debate: Livy's claim that he was a butcher's son is aristocratic slander.

people.name: Marcus Minucius Rufus
people.summary: Consul 221 (Istrian war); master of horse to Fabius in 217, then raised to equal imperium by the Lex Metilia and nearly destroyed at Gerunium; killed at Cannae. An altar he dedicated to Hercules calls him dictator.

people.name: Tiberius Sempronius Longus
people.summary: Consul 218, recalled from preparing an invasion of Africa at Lilybaeum to face Hannibal in the north, and defeated at the Trebia.

people.name: Publius Cornelius Scipio
people.summary: Father of Africanus. As consul 218 he missed Hannibal at the Rhône but sent his army on to Spain, was wounded at the Ticinus, and from 217 fought in Spain alongside his brother Gnaeus until both were killed in 211.
people.death: killed near Castulo in the battle of the Upper Baetis

people.name: Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Calvus
people.summary: Consul 222 (captured Mediolanum), who from 218 led the Roman war in Spain, winning at Cissa, the Ebro and Dertosa; killed at Ilorci in 211 after his Celtiberian mercenaries deserted.

people.name: Scipio Africanus
people.summary: The general who won the Second Punic War. Given the Spanish command at 25 as a privatus, he took New Carthage, won at Baecula and Ilipa and drove Carthage from Spain; as consul (205) he invaded Africa, destroyed the armies of Syphax and Hasdrubal, and defeated Hannibal at Zama (202). Later censor and princeps senatus, legate to his brother against Antiochus, and target of political trials, he died in self-imposed exile at Liternum.
people.detail: Polybius, writing for Scipio's adoptive grandson and drawing on Laelius, insists that Scipio's successes came from calculation and that he only exploited the popular belief in his divine inspiration. Livy preserves the legends: daily visits to the Capitoline temple, a serpent father like Alexander. His career strained republican norms (command without office, consulship under age, a cognomen from a conquered land) and he became the model for later great men. Polybius' and Livy's portraits both shaped the Renaissance image of the virtuous general.
people.death: died at his villa at Liternum
scholarship: Scullard, Scipio Africanus: Soldier and Politician (1970)

people.name: Gaius Laelius
people.summary: Scipio Africanus' lifelong friend and lieutenant: commander of the fleet at New Carthage, of the cavalry at Zama, captor of Syphax; consul 190. In old age he gave Polybius his eyewitness account of Scipio.

people.name: Gaius Laelius Sapiens
people.summary: Son of Africanus' friend and the closest friend of Scipio Aemilianus, whom he served at Carthage (stormed the Cothon, took Nepheris); consul 140. A cultivated orator and Stoic sympathiser, he is the speaker of Cicero's De amicitia.

people.name: Gaius Claudius Nero
people.summary: Consul 207, whose secret forced march north from Apulia brought about the destruction of Hasdrubal at the Metaurus; censor 204 with his enemy Livius Salinator. Ancestor of the Claudii Nerones and so of the emperor Tiberius.

people.name: Marcus Livius Salinator
people.summary: Consul 219 and victor in the Second Illyrian War, then convicted of unfairly dividing booty and retired in bitterness; recalled, he was consul again in 207 and shared the victory of the Metaurus. As censor in 204 he feuded with his colleague Nero.

people.name: Quintus Fulvius Flaccus
people.summary: Four times consul (237, 224, 212, 209), dictator 210 and conqueror of Capua (211), where he executed the Campanian senators, by tradition before the Senate's letter of clemency could be opened.

people.name: Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus
people.summary: Master of horse 216, consul 215 and 213, who led the slave legions (volones) to victory at Beneventum (214) and freed them; killed in an ambush in Lucania in 212.
people.death: killed in an ambush in Lucania

people.name: Marcus Valerius Laevinus
people.summary: Commander in the Adriatic who checked Philip V at Apollonia (214), concluded the alliance with the Aetolians (211) and, as consul 210, completed the conquest of Sicily by taking Agrigentum.

people.name: Publius Sulpicius Galba Maximus
people.summary: Consul 211 and commander in the First Macedonian War (sack of Aegina); as consul again in 200 he persuaded the reluctant comitia to vote for war on Philip V. Dictator 203.

people.name: Titus Quinctius Flamininus
people.summary: Consul at about 30 in 198, victor at the Aous and Cynoscephalae, and proclaimer of the freedom of the Greeks at the Isthmian Games of 196. Fluent in Greek, he was worshipped in Greek cities and was the first living Roman shown on a coin. In 183 he pressed Prusias to surrender Hannibal.
people.detail: Badian's study framed him as an adroit manipulator for whom philhellenism served Realpolitik and personal ambition; Polybius admired his diplomatic skill. His brother Lucius was expelled from the Senate by Cato.
scholarship: Badian, Titus Quinctius Flamininus: Philhellenism and Realpolitik (1970)

people.name: Manius Acilius Glabrio
people.summary: Novus homo and consul 191, who defeated Antiochus III at Thermopylae and besieged the Aetolians at Heraclea and Naupactus; vowed the temple of Pietas, which held the first gilded equestrian statue in Rome. His candidacy for the censorship in 189 was destroyed by charges of embezzlement backed by Cato.

people.name: Lucius Cornelius Scipio Asiaticus
people.summary: Younger brother of Africanus, consul 190, nominal victor at Magnesia over Antiochus III and holder of the cognomen Asiaticus. Prosecuted for misappropriating Seleucid money, fined, and deprived of his public horse by Cato in 184.

people.name: Gnaeus Manlius Vulso
people.summary: Consul 189, who campaigned against the Galatians without clear authorisation and supervised the Treaty of Apamea. His troops' Asiatic booty was blamed by Livy for introducing luxury to Rome.

people.name: Marcus Fulvius Nobilior
people.summary: Consul 189, conqueror of Ambracia and peacemaker with the Aetolians, patron of Ennius, who accompanied his campaign. He built the temple of Hercules Musarum with the looted Muses and a calendar with commentary, and as censor 179 the Basilica Aemilia et Fulvia.

people.name: Scipio Nasica
people.summary: Son of Gnaeus Scipio Calvus, judged the 'best man' in Rome and chosen to receive the Magna Mater at Ostia in 204; as consul 191 he completed the subjugation of the Boii.

people.name: Scipio Nasica Corculum
people.summary: Son of Nasica (cos. 191) and son-in-law of Africanus; distinguished at Pydna, consul 162 and 155 (took Delminium), censor 159, pontifex maximus from 150. He had the first stone theatre demolished and opposed Cato's call to destroy Carthage, arguing that fear of Carthage kept Rome disciplined.

people.name: Cato the Elder
people.summary: Novus homo from Tusculum who rose by talent and self-advertisement to consul (195) and censor (184). Hero of Thermopylae (191), scourge of the Scipios, prosecutor or defendant in some 44 trials, champion of old Roman frugality against Greek luxury (while learning Greek himself), author of the first Latin prose history (Origines), the earliest surviving Latin prose work (De agri cultura) and some 150 published speeches. He spent his last years demanding the destruction of Carthage.
people.detail: Cato's writings fixed the image of the stern, self-made Roman for posterity. His De agri cultura describes a slave-run estate of 100-240 iugera producing wine and oil for market, a document of the agrarian transformation of Italy. Astin argues that his anti-Hellenism was selective and political rather than a blanket rejection of Greek culture.

people.name: Lucius Valerius Flaccus
people.summary: Patrician patron who launched Cato's career, his colleague as consul (195) and censor (184), and princeps senatus from 184 until he died in the plague of 180.

people.name: Marcus Aemilius Lepidus
people.summary: Envoy who delivered Rome's ultimatum to Philip V at Abydos (200); consul 187 (Via Aemilia) and 175, censor 179, pontifex maximus from 180 and princeps senatus from 179, the most honoured senator of his generation. A later family coin shows him crowning Ptolemy V as guardian.
people.debate: The guardianship of Ptolemy V is attested only by Valerius Maximus and a late coin and may be family legend.

people.name: Lucius Aemilius Paullus Macedonicus
people.summary: Son of the consul killed at Cannae; governor of Ulterior (decree of Lascuta, 189), consul 182 and 168, victor of Pydna over Perseus, executor of the sack of Epirus and reorganiser of Macedonia. His triumph of 167 brought enough booty to end the citizen property tax; his two younger sons died around it. Father of Scipio Aemilianus and Fabius Aemilianus by adoption.
people.detail: Polybius, tutor to his sons, portrays him as the model of old Roman virtue and incorruptibility; at his death his estate barely covered his widow's dowry. He was also a connoisseur who took Perseus' library and erected a monument at Delphi.

people.name: Scipio Aemilianus
people.fullName: Publius Cornelius Scipio Aemilianus Africanus Numantinus
people.summary: Natural son of Aemilius Paullus, adopted by Africanus' son; fought at Pydna at 17, won the mural crown at Intercatia, destroyed Carthage (146) as consul under age, and as consul again in 134 besieged and razed Numantia. Patron of Polybius, Panaetius, Terence, Lucilius and the so-called Scipionic circle. Censor 142. He died suddenly in 129 amid the Gracchan crisis, rumour said by murder.
people.detail: Polybius was his mentor and companion at Carthage, and Cicero made him the ideal statesman of De re publica. His career, with dispensations from age limits and the iteration ban, illustrates the tension between republican rules and the demand for proven commanders. He opposed the Gracchan land commission's work on behalf of the Italian allies. 'Scipionic circle' as a cultural programme is largely Cicero's construction.
people.death: found dead in his bed in 129; murder suspected but never proven

people.name: Quintus Caecilius Metellus Macedonicus
people.summary: Praetor who defeated Andriscus at Pydna (148) and the Achaeans at Scarpheia (146); builder of the first marble temple in Rome (Jupiter Stator) and the Porticus Metelli; consul 143 in Spain, censor 131. He died having seen four sons reach the consulship, a byword for good fortune.

people.name: Lucius Mummius Achaicus
people.summary: Novus homo, praetor in Ulterior (153), consul 146, destroyer of Corinth, first new man to earn a victory cognomen. Remembered both as an honest administrator in Greece and as a philistine who threatened to make shippers replace lost masterpieces. Censor 142 with Scipio Aemilianus.

people.name: Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus
people.summary: Tribune who protected Lucius Scipio from prison despite personal enmity; governor of Citerior who made the lasting Gracchan treaties with the Celtiberians and founded Gracchurris; consul 177 (Sardinian war) and 163, censor 169. He married Cornelia, daughter of Africanus, and fathered the tribunes Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus.

people.name: Servius Sulpicius Galba
people.summary: Praetor in Ulterior who massacred the disarmed Lusitanians in 150; prosecuted in 149 with Cato against him, he was acquitted by parading his weeping children. Cicero rated him the finest orator of his day. Consul 144.

people.name: Quintus Fabius Maximus Servilianus
people.summary: Adopted into the Fabii; consul 142, who campaigned against Viriathus and, trapped at Erisane in 140, concluded the peace recognising him as a friend of the Roman people.

people.name: Quintus Servilius Caepio
people.summary: Consul 140 and brother of Servilianus, who repudiated his brother's peace, renewed the war and procured the murder of Viriathus by bribing his envoys (139).

people.name: Gaius Hostilius Mancinus
people.summary: Consul 137 who surrendered his army of 20,000 to the Numantines. The Senate disowned his treaty and in 136 had him handed over naked and bound by the fetials; the Numantines refused him. He commissioned a statue of himself in that state.

people.name: Decimus Junius Brutus Callaicus
people.summary: Consul 138, imprisoned by a tribune over the levy; founder of Valentia for Viriathus' veterans and conqueror of Gallaecia, where he led his men across the dreaded 'Lethe'. Patron of the tragic poet Accius.

people.name: Gaius Popillius Laenas
people.summary: Consul 172 (with the first all-plebeian college) and 158, who as envoy in 168 drew a circle around Antiochus IV at Eleusis and forced him out of Egypt.

people.name: Lucius Anicius Gallus
people.summary: Praetor 168 who conquered Genthius' Illyria in thirty days; at his triumphal games he made famous Greek flute-players fight like boxers to amuse the crowd (Polybius 30.22). Consul 160.

people.name: Lucius Licinius Lucullus
people.summary: Consul 151, imprisoned by tribunes over the levy, who then waged an unauthorised war on the Vaccaei and massacred the surrendered men of Cauca. He built a temple of Felicitas with Mummius' Greek statues.

people.name: Manius Manilius
people.summary: Consul 149 and commander at the beginning of the siege of Carthage; one of the founders of Roman civil law (Ulpian lists him with Brutus and Scaevola) and a speaker in Cicero's De re publica.

people.name: Lucius Marcius Censorinus
people.summary: Consul 149 who delivered to the disarmed Carthaginians the order to abandon their city, and then failed in his assaults on the walls. Censor 147.

people.name: Lucius Calpurnius Piso Frugi
people.summary: Tribune 149 who created the first standing court for extortion (Lex Calpurnia), consul 133 against the Sicilian slaves, censor 120, opponent of Gaius Gracchus and author of moralising Annales that dated the onset of luxury to 154.

people.name: Publius Rupilius
people.summary: Consul 132, friend of Scipio Aemilianus, who crushed the Sicilian slave revolt at Tauromenium and Enna and gave Sicily the Lex Rupilia; he prosecuted the followers of Tiberius Gracchus and died soon after his brother failed in a consular election.

people.name: Quintus Fabius Pictor
people.summary: Senator who served in the Gallic war of 225 and was sent to Delphi after Cannae; author, in Greek, of the first history of Rome by a Roman, presenting Rome's case to the Hellenistic world and blaming the Second Punic War on Barcid ambition. Polybius used and criticised him.
scholarship: Dillery, 'Quintus Fabius Pictor and Greco-Roman Historiography at Rome', in Miller et al. (eds.), Vertis in usum (2002)

people.name: Livius Andronicus
people.summary: Greek from Tarentum, probably brought to Rome as a captive and freed by a Livius; staged the first Latin tragedy and comedy at the Ludi Romani of 240, translated the Odyssey into Saturnian verse (Odusia) and composed the state hymn of 207.

people.name: Ennius
people.summary: Poet from Rudiae in Calabria, speaking Oscan, Greek and Latin ('three hearts'); brought to Rome by Cato, patronised by Fulvius Nobilior and the Scipios, granted citizenship in 184. His Annales, in Latin hexameters, told Roman history from Aeneas to his own day and was the national epic until Virgil.
scholarship: Skutsch, The Annals of Quintus Ennius (1985)

people.name: Plautus
people.summary: Umbrian from Sarsina, the most popular comic dramatist of Rome; 21 comedies adapted from Greek New Comedy survive, full of song, wordplay and Roman references (Miles Gloriosus, Pseudolus, Menaechmi, Amphitruo).

people.name: Terence
people.summary: Former slave from Carthaginian Africa who wrote six polished comedies after Menander and Apollodorus (166-160), close to the circle of Scipio Aemilianus and Laelius; he died on a journey to Greece.
people.debate: His birth date (195 or 185) is uncertain.
